extracted.intended_audience: law students and patent practitioners studying patentable subject matter (§101) issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and doctrinal criteria for determining whether claimed subject matter (especially processes, business methods, and computer-implemented inventions) is eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101. The excerpt canvasses textual, historical, and functional tests and examples from Supreme Court jurisprudence (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are close to 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' do not count as 'processes' under § 101 and are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Diamond v. Diehr and Gottschalk v. Benson: phenomena of nature, mental processes, and abstract intellectual concepts are basic tools of scientific and technological work and cannot be patented because allowing patents would 'wholly pre-empt' public access to those tools. Prevents blocking follow-on innovation. Examples/anti-patterns: mental processes and fundamental principles should be excluded; courts should avoid patents that effectively monopolize these basic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as an important clue
rubrics_metrics.description: The transformation and reduction of an article to a different state or thing is a clue to the patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Diehr and Flook: when a claim transforms an article or reduces it to a different state, that's a strong indicator of patent eligibility. The test has been repeatedly helpful to courts in deciding what constitutes a patentable 'process.' However, it is a clue, not necessarily dispositive (see next entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is not the sole test
rubrics_metrics.description: Although useful and important, the machine-or-transformation test has never been the exclusive test for § 101 patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benson rejects treating the test as the only pathway to process patentability. Courts should consider claims 'as a whole' and not rigidly exclude processes that do not literally transform an article or recite a particular machine. The Federal Circuit erred where it treated the test as the exclusive standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'process' in §101 by patent-law historical usage (not ordinary sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'process' in § 101 has a distinctive meaning in patent law developed against a historical background and should not be read in its wide ordinary sense (which would encompass everyday methods like dog training or dance steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual interpretation should account for terms of art and historical practice. Relying solely on 'ordinary, contemporary, common meaning' risks absurd results and overbroad eligibility; courts should heed historical norms shaping the patent categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods are not patentable 'processes' under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of steps for conducting business—i.e., business methods—are not, in themselves, 'processes' within the meaning of § 101 and historically were not considered patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by historical evidence from English and early American practice, treatises, and Supreme Court reasoning; courts should be cautious about treating business organization, management techniques, or methods of conducting commerce as patentable subject matter. Examples/anti-patterns: patents directed merely to business organization or financial techniques (without more) are properly excluded. The State Street decision and later developments are discussed as departures or limited decisions addressing machines/software claims rather than pure business methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a generic computer does not make an abstract idea patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely requiring generic computer implementation of an abstract idea fails to transform that abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Alice: a computer-implemented scheme for intermediated settlement was held drawn to an abstract idea; generic computer implementation added nothing inventive. Anti-pattern: drafting claims that tack on a 'computer' or 'server' without adding a specific improvement in computer technology will not save an otherwise abstract claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claims 'as a whole' when evaluating §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim meets § 101 when, considered as a whole, it performs a function the patent laws were designed to protect (for example, transforming or reducing an article to a different state or thing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not dissect claims into insubstantial post-solution activity; holistic analysis (Diehr) can show that a claim embodies patentable subject matter even if some elements are abstract when isolated. Conversely, holistic analysis can reveal when the claim is essentially an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional/functional balance: promotion of the 'useful arts' limits scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility must be interpreted in light of the constitutional purpose to 'promote the Progress of . . . useful Arts'—a balance between encouraging innovation and avoiding monopolies that stifle competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh whether granting patents in a category (e.g., business methods) would more likely promote or impede progress. Factors include the costs/risks of innovation in the field, the benefits of public disclosure, and potential chilling effects on follow-on innovation. Historical practice and policy concerns inform this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic-policy considerations about incentives and necessity of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether patents are necessary to motivate innovation in a field is relevant to whether patents should be recognized, particularly when innovation can be achieved through other means (trade secrecy, first-mover advantages, branding, network effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and policymakers should consider empirical/economic evidence (e.g., many business innovations have occurred without patents, like Federal Express) and whether the category involves high R&D costs and easy copying (which favor patent incentives). This analysis can counsel against broad patentability in areas where patents add little incentive but high social costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of vagueness and breadth for business method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Business method patents tend to be broad, intangible, and potentially vague, making it costly and time-consuming to search, negotiate licenses, and avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because clarity is essential to promote progress, patents that claim intangible, widely-applicable steps can impose high informational and transaction costs on industry and may enable bullying litigation even when ultimately invalid. Anti-pattern: granting broad, high-level patents that cover 'big ideas' near the top of the knowledge pyramid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty, nonobviousness, and written-description requirements cannot alone confine §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of novelty, nonobviousness, and particular description (e.g., § 112) cannot be relied upon to rescue § 101 from overbroad or absurd results; they do not substitute for proper subject-matter limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim is novel or nonobvious, it might still be an improper subject for a patent if it falls into excluded categories (abstract idea, law of nature). Historical examples show many human activities could be novel yet inappropriate for patent monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Anything under the sun' legislative history cannot be read to allow all processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The oft-cited legislative history phrase that the subject matter includes 'anything under the sun that is made by man' has been misread; it does not mean that any series of steps is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical clues and higher-level interpretive context constrain any broad reading of that phrase. Courts should not treat the phrase as eliminating established subject-matter limits reflected in historical practice and Supreme Court precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Inventor Defense Act §273 does not ratify business-method patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1999 First Inventor Defense Act (§ 273) provides a limited defense to infringement for certain methods of doing business but was not intended to, and does not, expand § 101 to make business methods patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act's content and history show it was a limited fix to mitigate fallout from State Street-type holdings rather than a congressional endorsement of sweeping business-method patentability; courts should not read it as an amendment to § 101's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding preemption of fundamental tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent doctrine must avoid granting rights that 'pre-empt' the public's use of basic tools (e.g., fundamental ideas or business tools) necessary for scientific, technological, or commercial work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption concerns justify categorical exclusions (laws of nature, abstract ideas) because allowing patents on such basics would block downstream innovation. Courts should assess whether a claim would unduly preempt a fundamental building block of further work.
